title: General Bézout Solution Set: The Non-Coprime Coset Classification
description: The parent entry classifies the solution set of a·x + b·y = c for coprime a, b as one coset of the rank-1 lattice ℤ·(b, −a). This entry resolves its first open question: drop coprimality. For arbitrary a, b (not both zero) with g = gcd(a,b), writing a = g·a', b = g·b' with a', b' coprime, the solution set of a·x + b·y = c is solvable iff g ∣ c, and is exactly one coset of the PRIMITIVE lattice ℤ·(b', −a') = ℤ·(b/g, −a/g) — not the non-primitive ℤ·(b, −a). It proves the general homogeneous lemma, uniqueness, the converse parametrization, the solvability criterion, the existence of the primitive decomposition from Mathlib's integer gcd (Int.exists_gcd_one'), a packaged uniqueness statement for arbitrary integers, and worked instances for the non-coprime pair (6, 9).

The packaged statements assume b ≠ 0 (so gcd > 0 and b' ≠ 0), exactly mirroring the parent entry's scope; the symmetric a ≠ 0 case follows by swapping roles.

overview.historicalContext: The classification of linear Diophantine equations a·x + b·y = c is classical: solvability is governed by gcd(a,b) (Bézout's solvability criterion, implicit in Euclid and made explicit through the extended Euclidean algorithm), and the solution set, when non-empty, is a one-parameter family. Mathlib captures solvability as Int.gcd_dvd_iff (gcd a b ∣ n ↔ ∃ x y, n = a·x + b·y) and supplies the primitive decomposition a = a'·g, b = b'·g with gcd a' b' = 1 via Int.exists_gcd_one'. What Mathlib does not package is the full description of the solution SET as a coset of a specific lattice. The parent entry supplied that coset description in the coprime case; this entry completes it for arbitrary a, b — the precise content of the parent's first open question.
overview.problemStatement: Drop coprimality from the parent classification. For arbitrary integers a, b not both zero, with g = gcd(a,b) and a = g·a', b = g·b' (a', b' coprime, the primitive cofactors a/g, b/g): show (i) a·x + b·y = c is solvable iff g ∣ c, and (ii) the solution set, when non-empty, is exactly one coset {(x₀ + k·b', y₀ − k·a') : k ∈ ℤ} of the PRIMITIVE rank-1 lattice ℤ·(b', −a'). Connect the decomposition to Mathlib's actual integer gcd and package a uniqueness statement that takes only a, b : ℤ with b ≠ 0.
overview.proofStrategy: Everything reduces to the coprime core after stripping the common factor g. general_homogeneous: from a·u + b·v = 0 with a = g·a', b = g·b', factor out g to get g·(a'·u + b'·v) = 0; since g ≠ 0, a'·u + b'·v = 0, and the coprime argument (b' ∣ a'·u, coprimality upgrades to b' ∣ u via IsCoprime.dvd_of_dvd_mul_left, then cancel b' ≠ 0) yields (u,v) = (k·b', −k·a'). The lattice is generated by the PRIMITIVE vector (b', −a'), which is the crucial difference from the naïve (b, −a). general_unique differences two solutions to land in the homogeneous case; general_param is a one-line ring identity. general_solvable_iff: forward, a·x + b·y = g·(a'·x + b'·y) is a multiple of g; backward, coprimality gives u·a' + v·b' = 1 (IsCoprime), so scaling by c/g yields an explicit solution. int_admits_decomp produces g, a', b' from Int.exists_gcd_one' (with g = gcd a b > 0 because b ≠ 0, shown via gcd_dvd_right and zero_dvd_iff), transporting coprimality through Int.isCoprime_iff_gcd_eq_one. int_general_unique packages it: any two solutions of a·x + b·y = c differ by one step of ℤ·(b/g, −a/g).
keyInsights: The lattice generated by the homogeneous solutions is the PRIMITIVE one ℤ·(b', −a') = ℤ·(b/g, −a/g), NOT ℤ·(b, −a). For (6,9) the step is (3, −2), not (9, −6): the non-primitive vector would miss two-thirds of the solutions. This is the substantive correction coprimality hides.

Generality costs nothing structural: stripping the common factor g (using only g ≠ 0 and a single linear_combination) reduces the entire non-coprime problem to the already-proved coprime core. Number theory enters in exactly one place — b' ∣ a'·u ⟹ b' ∣ u via coprimality.

Solvability and the coset structure are independent facts: a·x + b·y = c is solvable iff g ∣ c (general_solvable_iff), and WHEN solvable its solution set is a full coset of ℤ·(b', −a') (general_unique + general_param). The example 6·x + 9·y = 7 is unsolvable precisely because 3 ∤ 7.

Int.exists_gcd_one' is the bridge from the abstract decomposition hypotheses to concrete integers: it furnishes g = gcd(a,b) and the primitive cofactors with gcd a' b' = 1, which Int.isCoprime_iff_gcd_eq_one turns into IsCoprime a' b'.

The b ≠ 0 hypothesis is exactly what guarantees both g = gcd(a,b) > 0 and b' ≠ 0; it mirrors the parent entry's scope, and the symmetric a ≠ 0 statement is obtained by swapping the roles of the two coordinates.

sections.title: General (Non-Coprime) Classification of the Linear Diophantine Solution Set
sections.summary: The parent entry classifies the Bézout solution set of a*x+b*y=c only for coprime a,b. This file drops that hypothesis: for arbitrary a,b (not both zero) with g=gcd(a,b), write a=g*a', b=g*b' with a',b' coprime. Then a*x+b*y=c is solvable iff g divides c, and the full solution set is one coset of the primitive lattice Z*(b',-a'), not the naive Z*(b,-a). Delivers general_homogeneous, general_unique/param, general_solvable_iff, int_admits_decomp, and int_general_unique, with worked non-coprime instance (6,9). 0 axioms, 0 sorries.
sections.mathContext: Writing $a=ga',b=gb'$ with $a',b'$ coprime: $ax+by=c$ solvable $\iff g\mid c$, and the solution set is one coset of the primitive lattice $\mathbb{Z}\cdot(b',-a')$, not the naive $\mathbb{Z}\cdot(b,-a)$.

sections.title: General Homogeneous Solutions
sections.summary: general_homogeneous: for a = g·a', b = g·b' (g ≠ 0, a' b' coprime, b' ≠ 0), every solution of a·u + b·v = 0 is the primitive lattice point (k·b', −k·a'). Strips g then runs the coprime divisibility argument.

sections.title: Uniqueness and Parametrization
sections.summary: general_unique: two solutions of a·x + b·y = c differ by one primitive step (k·b', −k·a'), via differencing into the homogeneous case. general_param: the converse ring identity a·(x + k·b') + b·(y − k·a') = a·x + b·y.

sections.title: Solvability Criterion
sections.summary: general_solvable_iff: a·x + b·y = c is solvable iff g ∣ c. Forward by factoring out g; backward by scaling the coprime Bézout witness u·a' + v·b' = 1.

sections.title: Connecting to the Integer gcd
sections.summary: int_admits_decomp: every a, b : ℤ with b ≠ 0 admits a primitive decomposition (g = gcd > 0, a' b' coprime, b' ≠ 0) from Int.exists_gcd_one'. int_general_unique: packaged uniqueness — two solutions differ by one step of ℤ·(b/g, −a/g).

sections.title: Worked Instances — Non-Coprime Pair (6, 9)
sections.summary: gcd(6,9)=3, primitive cofactors (a',b')=(2,3), primitive lattice ℤ·(3,−2). Two solutions of 6·x+9·y=12 differing by k=−1, the full family, and the unsolvability of 6·x+9·y=7 (since 3∤7).

conclusion.summary: For arbitrary integers a, b (b ≠ 0) with g = gcd(a,b), the linear Diophantine equation a·x + b·y = c is solvable iff g ∣ c, and its solution set is then exactly one coset of the PRIMITIVE rank-1 lattice ℤ·(b/g, −a/g). The whole result reduces to the coprime case by stripping the common factor g; the connection to Mathlib's integer gcd is made via Int.exists_gcd_one'. Fully machine-checked, 0 axioms, 0 sorries.
conclusion.implications: This completes the parent entry's classification by removing the coprimality hypothesis, pinning down the precise (primitive) lattice of ambiguity for any linear Diophantine equation in two variables. The general_homogeneous lemma is a reusable building block for linear Diophantine reasoning over ℤ where the coefficients share a factor.
openQuestions: Identify the canonical/minimal solution (the reduced representative with |y| < |a/g|/2) and prove the extended Euclidean algorithm returns it.
Extend the primitive-lattice description to k-variable systems a₁x₁ + … + a_kx_k = c, whose solution set is a coset of a rank-(k−1) lattice spanned by primitive vectors.
Formalize the smith-normal-form view: the solution set of a single linear equation over ℤ as the kernel-plus-particular decomposition produced by integer row reduction.

crossReferences.description: Parent entry classifies the Bézout solution set for COPRIME a, b as a coset of ℤ·(b, −a). This entry drops coprimality, replacing it with the primitive lattice ℤ·(b/g, −a/g) for general a, b — the parent's first open question.
Grandparent line develops Bézout → Euclid's Lemma → FTA. This entry supplies the general linear-Diophantine solution-set classification underneath that chain.
